meta.title: Monitoring Model Drift and Quality
meta.thesis: Monitoring Model Drift and Quality is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A deployed classifier and LLM assistant degrade as customer questions and product docs change. By the end, they should be able to build or review drift and quality monitor with alerts and review queues, measure time from quality drop to triage, and catch the failure where aggregate metrics stay flat while a high-value segment fails.

modules.title: Monitor decisions, not just endpoints
modules.sub: Define what quality means after deployment and which evidence can arrive late.
modules.summary: A model can be available and fast while its decisions become wrong, biased, stale, or expensive.
objectives: Distinguish system health from model quality.
Name data drift, prediction drift, concept drift, and performance decay.
Define the owner and action for alerts.

blocks.title: Healthy software can serve bad predictions

spans.text: Problem anchor: a loan pre-screen model returns responses in 80 ms with no server errors, yet approval quality deteriorates after a new marketing campaign changes applicant mix. Uptime dashboards are green while the model is wrong for a growing slice of traffic.

Monitoring model quality means watching more than infrastructure. Data drift asks whether inputs changed. Prediction drift asks whether outputs changed. Concept drift asks whether the relationship between inputs and outcomes changed. Performance decay asks whether users or business outcomes got worse, often after labels arrive days or weeks later.

items.text: Product framing: monitoring protects decisions and user trust.
Engineering framing: monitoring joins request logs, model version, features, predictions, labels, and latency.
Operations framing: every alert needs severity, owner, playbook, and rollback or investigation path.

spans.text: The release card says model v42 is live. The monitoring target records application channel, region, employment type, score band, decision, latency, model version, and later repayment or manual-review outcome. Reference window: last stable 14 days after v42 rollout. Alert slices: new applicants, self-employed, region, campaign source, and protected-class proxies only where policy allows.
The output of monitoring is not "drift detected." It is a decision: investigate data pipeline, adjust thresholds, retrain, roll back, or add human review for a slice.

blocks.title: Green service, bad model
blocks.prompt: What can be true when uptime and latency dashboards are green?

options.text: The model is automatically high quality.
The model can still be wrong because data, labels, or user behavior shifted.
No monitoring beyond CPU and memory is needed.

blocks.explanation: Production model quality depends on live data and outcomes, not only service health.

modules.title: Choose reference windows and slices
modules.sub: Compare live traffic to a meaningful baseline and avoid aggregate blindness.
modules.summary: Drift checks are useful only when the reference window, slice definitions, and sample sizes match the decision.
objectives: Select a reference window for drift monitoring.
Explain why aggregate metrics hide cohort failures.
Connect delayed labels to monitoring design.

blocks.title: The baseline is a decision, not a default

spans.text: A reference window can be training data, a recent stable production period, or an approved benchmark. Training data may be too old; yesterday may include an incident; a benchmark may miss seasonal traffic. Choose deliberately and record why.

Slices matter because aggregate stability can hide harm. A recommender may look fine overall while new users fail. A fraud model may improve global precision while missing a new merchant type. A chatbot may keep average satisfaction while one language regresses.

blocks.title: Case study: aggregate hides a regional failure

spans.text: Overall approval precision moves from .81 to .80, below the alert threshold. In one region, precision drops from .79 to .62 after a new data vendor starts filling missing employment length with zeros. A slice alert catches what the global metric hides.
This recalls module 1: monitoring protects decisions. If the decision affects a cohort, the monitoring view must be able to see that cohort within privacy and policy boundaries.

modules.title: Add LLM quality signals to ML monitoring
modules.sub: Track prompts, retrieval, route policy, cost, latency, safety, and human feedback for generative systems.
modules.summary: LLM apps need classic service and drift signals plus traces for prompts, retrieval, model routes, guardrails, and evaluations.
objectives: Explain why route and cache status affect quality.
Design alerts that lead to action rather than noise.

blocks.title: Generative monitoring has more moving parts

spans.text: For an LLM support assistant, quality can change because the prompt changed, retrieval index refreshed, model route switched, semantic cache reused stale content, a tool schema broke, or policy filters became stricter. Traditional accuracy labels may arrive slowly or not at all, so traces and eval samples become core monitoring evidence.

Useful dimensions include model and response model, prompt version, retrieval index version, top-k citations, tool outcome, guardrail action, refusal rate, token usage, cost, latency, route, cache hit, fallback chain, and user feedback. OpenTelemetry-style GenAI attributes give teams a shared vocabulary for many of these fields.

blocks.title: Worked LLM dashboard for lesson generation

spans.text: Dashboard rows group by prompt version, model route, retrieval index, and lesson category. Signals: validation pass rate, citation coverage, editor rejection rate, average tokens, p95 render latency, safety intervention rate, and top regression examples. A spike in cost with stable pass rate may be acceptable; a stable cost with lower citation coverage is not.
The alert message should name the owner and next action: "RAG citation coverage for Safety lessons dropped below 92 percent after index kb_v12; run retrieval smoke set and hold enrichment releases."

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Alert on product-relevant movement, not every statistical wiggle.
blocks.useWhen: Use LLM monitoring when prompt, model, route, retrieval, or safety policy changes can affect users without code deploys.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid paging humans for tiny distribution shifts without severity, sample size, slice, and playbook.

blocks.title: Minimal drift alert skeleton

spans.text: The code deliberately combines magnitude, sample size, version, slice, and owner. A real system would use a monitoring library or platform, but the alert contract is the teaching point.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Why is `sample_size >= 500` included before a high-severity alert?
predictThenReveal.answer: Without a sample-size guard, tiny windows can create noisy alerts that look severe but are not reliable enough for action.

spans.text: Review AI-generated monitoring advice for missing operational pieces. It should name reference windows, slices, sample-size rules, model and prompt versions, delayed-label joins, privacy limits, thresholds, owners, playbooks, and rollback or retraining criteria.

items.text: Does the plan monitor data, predictions, outcomes, and service behavior?
Can every alert be sliced by release version and relevant cohort?
Does it avoid storing raw sensitive text or features unless redaction and retention are defined?
Does the playbook say investigate, roll back, retrain, adjust threshold, or add human review?

blocks.title: Privacy in monitoring
blocks.prompt: What is a common monitoring risk for LLM apps?

options.text: Latency metrics always reveal private data.
Trace logs can capture sensitive prompts or retrieved content without redaction and retention policy.
Monitoring eliminates the need for evals.

blocks.explanation: Monitoring payloads need governance because they may contain user text, features, or decisions.

blocks.title: Retrieval prompt for the whole lesson

spans.text: Answer this from memory: "How do I monitor whether a deployed model is still useful?" Include service health, data drift, prediction drift, concept drift, delayed labels, slices, reference windows, LLM traces, privacy controls, owners, and playbooks.
Spaced recall: module 1 warned that healthy software can serve bad predictions. The final monitoring loop exists to catch that gap and choose a response with evidence.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: A drift alert is a question, not an automatic retrain button.
blocks.useWhen: Use monitoring to trigger investigation, rollback, threshold review, human review, or retraining based on evidence.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid retraining blindly from every distribution shift; some shifts are expected, harmless, or caused by instrumentation changes.

spans.text: Choose a model or LLM feature. Define one reference window, three slices, two drift signals, one delayed-label metric, version fields, privacy limits, alert thresholds, owner, and first-response playbook. Then write the exact alert message a human should receive.
Next rung: connect this to model registries and versioning, where release identity lets monitoring point to the artifact or policy that changed.

gpu.label: GPU
gpu.laymanDefinition: The compute layer whose health can hide or amplify model-quality problems.
gpu.technicalNote: GPU saturation, queue time, or fallback to a different endpoint should be monitored alongside quality because infra changes can alter model behavior.

serving.label: Serving
serving.laymanDefinition: The production prediction path being monitored.
serving.technicalNote: Serving logs need model version, input summaries, prediction, decision, latency, errors, and later labels or feedback when available.

gateway.label: Gateway
gateway.laymanDefinition: The policy layer that can change which model or provider answers.
gateway.technicalNote: Gateway route, cache status, fallback chain, and model alias are monitoring dimensions for LLM and multi-model systems.

latency.label: Latency
latency.laymanDefinition: A reliability signal that can correlate with quality issues.
latency.technicalNote: Rising latency can indicate overload, longer prompts, fallback chains, retrieval slowdown, or a model version change.

throughput.label: Throughput
throughput.laymanDefinition: The volume of predictions or requests flowing through the system.
throughput.technicalNote: Monitoring windows must account for traffic volume because tiny samples and seasonal spikes can create false alarms.

versioning.label: Versioning
versioning.laymanDefinition: The link between monitoring signals and the release that produced them.
versioning.technicalNote: Every alert should be sliceable by model, prompt, retrieval index, feature code, route policy, and deployment version.

checklist.label: Does monitoring define quality, not only endpoint health?
Are reference windows, slices, sample-size rules, and delayed labels explicit?
Do LLM traces include prompt, route, retrieval, cache, cost, latency, and safety dimensions?
Does each alert name severity, owner, evidence, and first response?
Are privacy, redaction, and retention limits defined for monitoring payloads?

capstone.prompt: Create a one-page release-ready plan for drift and quality monitor with alerts and review queues. Include: the user problem, realistic input, mechanism, design choice, runnable or reviewable check, metric (time from quality drop to triage), failure case (aggregate metrics stay flat while a high-value segment fails), owner, and the next rung after this lesson.
